text: In GSoC participant Markdown files (e.g., `{year}/participants/{name}.md` and `{year}/{username}/README.md`), use descriptive Markdown hyperlinks (`[label](url)`) instead of bare URLs, link completed checklist items or researched resources to the specific artifacts they refer to (PR, issue, discussion, blog post, repo, demo), and keep lists properly formatted with valid Markdown syntax.
reason: Descriptive, well-formed links let reviewers verify progress and understand long resource lists without opening every URL, while making each participant file self-contained.
common_pattern: Documentation conventions for GSoC participant files: participant Markdown should be structured, scannable, and verifiable, using descriptive Markdown links/evidence and following the provided checklist/template.

text: In documentation markup (especially README files), ensure all external references are accurate, current, and accessible: link to stable/current documentation instead of version-pinned URLs, avoid hotlinking third-party assets, provide descriptive alt text for images and badges (naming the link destination or platform), and when reusing markup from another source, audit and adapt all URLs, image names, and alt text.
reason: Documentation quality: prevents misleading or broken references, accessibility issues, and licensing/attribution problems.
common_pattern: Ensuring accuracy, accessibility, and proper attribution of external references (links, images, alt text) in documentation markup.

text: Proofread documentation files (READMEs, including participant READMEs in `2023/{name}/README.md`) with a spellchecker and fix typos/grammatical errors before submitting a PR.
reason: Public-facing documentation with typos and grammatical errors reduces readability and perceived professionalism. (e.g., `Mastodown` → `Mastodon`, `Installating` → `Installing`)
common_pattern: Documentation (README files, especially participant READMEs) must be proofread/spellchecked before submission to fix typos and grammatical errors.

text: In README/participant checklist files, before marking a task complete, verify that the linked deliverable directly satisfies every stated criterion in the task description, including content match, recency, and any measurable requirements; replace links that are outdated, tangentially related, or fail the criteria.
reason: Prevents reviewers from accepting checklists where a task is marked done using a similarly named but non-compliant artifact.
common_pattern: Checklist tasks must only be marked complete when the linked deliverable actually satisfies every stated requirement in the task description.

text: When project documentation lists recommended learning resources or courses, include relevant authoritative external training links (e.g., official course pages).
reason: External courses provide structured, authoritative learning paths for readers researching or onboarding into the topic.
common_pattern: Both generalizations come from the same review comment and express the same documentation improvement: recommended learning-resource sections should include authoritative external course/training links. Generalization 2 is the file-specific instantiation of Generalization 1.

text: When linking repositories from a README (e.g., in a Research or portfolio/work section), only link publicly accessible repositories, and ensure each linked repository has its own README with enough detail for reviewers to understand the project.
reason: Readers and reviewers cannot access private repository links, and brief links without project-level documentation do not provide enough context to demonstrate or evaluate the claimed work.
common_pattern: Repository links included in a README should be useful to reviewers: the linked repository must be publicly accessible and should have its own README providing enough context and detail to understand the work.

text: Keep RFCs tightly scoped to the proposal's stated subject. Include background, prior-art, or adjacent-system context only when it directly informs the proposed design; remove or rewrite sections that do not directly support that subject (e.g., unrelated WordPress background details), and discuss adjacent mechanisms (e.g., scheduling/cron) only to explain how they affect the core feature. Write original project-specific prose rather than generic AI-generated boilerplate or padding.
reason: Scoped RFCs keep reviewers focused on the actual proposal, reduce noise, and maintain credibility by avoiding irrelevant surveys, tangential background, or boilerplate that obscure the intended design decision.
common_pattern: RFC and design-doc authoring should stay scoped to the stated topic, using only directly relevant background/prior art and avoiding adjacent-system drift or generic AI-generated prose.

text: In GSoC participant checklist files under `{year}/participants/{name}.md`, follow the provided task template exactly; do not add custom roadmap, milestone, or self-defined checklist sections without explicit approval, and include a Markdown table where the checklist or template calls for one.
reason: Custom sections can diverge from shared GSoC guidance and make it harder to track whether participants are following the expected contribution path, while required tables keep structured information scannable.
common_pattern: Documentation conventions for GSoC participant files: participant Markdown should be structured, scannable, and verifiable, using descriptive Markdown links/evidence and following the provided checklist/template.
